rows.stem:
Pravin was given a list of characteristics associated with the process of anaerobic respiration in humans, in the table given below :

|  | Location | Condition | End Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| Characteristic | (i) Muscle Cell | (ii) Requires presence of Oxygen \((\mathrm{O_2})\) and Carbon dioxide \((\mathrm{CO_2})\) | (iii) 3-Carbon molecules |

Which of the above characteristics is/are related to the above process ?

options.label: A
options.text: (i) and (ii)

options.label: B
options.text: (i) and (iii)

options.label: C
options.text: (ii) and (iii)

options.label: D
options.text: (i) only

rows.solution:
Anaerobic respiration in humans takes place in muscle cells during vigorous activity, when oxygen runs short. Glucose is broken down to pyruvate, a 3-carbon molecule, and the pyruvate is converted to lactic acid, also a 3-carbon molecule. It does not need oxygen, so characteristic (ii) does not belong to it.

So (i) and (iii) are related to the process, which is option (B) (i) and (iii).

rows.stem: Observe the figure given below and identify the *incorrect* step for the activity set-up :

options.label: A
options.text: Both plants are kept in the dark room for three days before placing them in separate glass jars.

options.label: B
options.text: Both plants are covered with separate wooden bell-jars.

options.label: C
options.text: Use vaseline to seal the bottom of the jars with the glass plates.

options.label: D
options.text: Both potted plants were kept in sunlight for a few hours before the iodine test for the presence of starch.

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the activity set-up is drawn: two potted plants (I) and (II), each under its own bell-jar, with a watch-glass containing potassium hydroxide (labelled) beside plant (I). Every option states its step in words, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
In this activity the plants are first kept in the dark for three days to remove their starch, then placed on glass plates and covered with bell-jars sealed at the bottom with vaseline, and kept in sunlight before the iodine test. The bell-jars must be of glass so that sunlight can reach the plants; a wooden bell-jar would block the light and no photosynthesis could take place in either plant.

The incorrect step is option (B) Both plants are covered with separate wooden bell-jars.

rows.subtopic: Human Brain and Protection of Nervous Tissue
rows.stem:
Walking in a straight line and riding a bicycle are activities which are possible due to coordination of which part of the brain ?

*(Part of the Brain)*, *(Name of the area of the Brain)*

options.label: A
options.text: Fore-Brain, Cerebrum

options.label: B
options.text: Mid-Brain, Cerebellum

options.label: C
options.text: Hind-Brain, Cerebellum

options.label: D
options.text: Hind-Brain, Medulla

rows.solution:
Walking in a straight line and riding a bicycle need posture and balance to be maintained and voluntary movements to be precise. This is the work of the cerebellum, which is part of the hind-brain.

This is option (C) Hind-Brain, Cerebellum.

rows.stem: In a synapse, the chemical signal is transmitted from :

options.label: A
options.text: Dendritic end of one neuron to axonal end of another neuron.

options.label: B
options.text: Axon to cell body of the same neuron.

options.label: C
options.text: Cell body to axonal end of the same neuron.

options.label: D
options.text: Axonal end of one neuron to dendritic end of another neuron.

rows.solution:
At a synapse the electrical impulse reaching the axonal end of one neuron releases chemicals. These cross the gap and start an electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.

This is option (D) Axonal end of one neuron to dendritic end of another neuron.

rows.stem: Organisms of a higher trophic level which feed on several types of organisms belonging to a lower trophic level form the :

options.label: A
options.text: Food web

options.label: B
options.text: Ecosystem

options.label: C
options.text: Ecological pyramid

options.label: D
options.text: Food chain

rows.solution:
When organisms of a higher trophic level feed on several kinds of organisms of a lower level, the food chains become interconnected and form a branching network, the food web.

This is option (A) Food web.

rows.stem: In accumulation of toxic substances at higher trophic levels of an ecosystem through the food chain, which of the following organisms is affected the most ?

options.label: A
options.text: Small aquatic plants

options.label: B
options.text: Human beings

options.label: C
options.text: Small fish

options.label: D
options.text: Large fish

rows.solution:
Toxic substances such as pesticides are not degradable, so they accumulate progressively at each trophic level (biological magnification). Human beings occupy the top level in most food chains, so the maximum concentration of these chemicals accumulates in them.

This is option (B) Human beings.

rows.stem: The growth of tendrils in grapes plants is due to :

options.label: A
options.text: Effect of light

options.label: B
options.text: Effect of gravity

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid cell division in tendril cells in contact with the support

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid cell division in tendril cells that are away from the support

rows.solution:
A tendril is sensitive to touch. When it comes in contact with a support, the part of the tendril in contact with the support does not grow as rapidly as the part away from it. The faster growth of the cells on the side away from the support makes the tendril coil around the support.

This is option (D) Rapid cell division in tendril cells that are away from the support.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Natural replenishment of soil will not take place in absence of microbes.

**Reason (R) :** Microbes, comprising of bacteria and fungi, break down dead remains and waste products of organisms, and they go into the soil.
rows.context: For Questions number 8 and 9, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Microbes such as bacteria and fungi decompose the dead remains and waste products of organisms, and the simple substances so formed go back into the soil. Without them the soil would not be replenished naturally, so the Assertion is true. The Reason states exactly this role of the decomposers, so it is true and explains the Assertion.

Both are true and the Reason is the correct explanation, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The basic filtration unit in the kidneys, like in the lungs, is a cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries.

**Reason (R) :** Each capillary cluster in the kidney is associated with the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube called Bowman’s capsule.
rows.context: For Questions number 8 and 9, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The basic filtration unit of the kidney, like the alveoli in the lungs, is a cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries, so the Assertion is true. Each such cluster in the kidney is associated with the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube, Bowman's capsule, so the Reason is true as well.

But the Reason only describes where the capillary cluster sits; it does not explain why the filtration unit is a cluster of thin-walled capillaries. Both are true and the Reason is not the correct explanation, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
(i) Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) have been linked to depletion of ozone layer. In 1987, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) succeeded in making an agreement. State this agreement.

(ii) What is the role of ozone in our atmosphere ?
rows.solution:
(i) The agreement made in 1987 under the United Nations Environment Programme was to freeze the production of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) at the 1986 levels.

(ii) Ozone in the upper atmosphere shields the surface of the earth from the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation of the sun.

rows.stem: What kind of respiration provides more energy and why ?
rows.solution:
Aerobic respiration provides more energy.

In aerobic respiration glucose is broken down completely, in the presence of oxygen, to carbon dioxide and water, and much more energy is released. In anaerobic respiration the breakdown is incomplete (to ethanol and carbon dioxide, or to lactic acid), so much less energy is released.

rows.stem:
Separation of right side and left side of the heart is useful to keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing. Various organisms have different types of heart.

(I) Fill in the blanks (i) to (iii) correctly according to the type of organisms and their evolution in terms of blood circulation :

| Organisms | Number of chambers in heart | Type of blood being circulated | Type of circulation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fish | (i) ______ | Mixed | Single |
| (ii) ______ | 3-chambered | Mixed | Incomplete double circulation |
| Birds and Mammals | 4-chambered | Separated circulation path of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood | (iii) ______ |

(II) Which type of circulation is most efficient ?
rows.solution:
(I) (i) 2-chambered. (ii) Amphibians (or reptiles). (iii) Double circulation.

(II) Double circulation, as in birds and mammals, is the most efficient: the oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix, so the body gets a highly efficient supply of oxygen.

The table prints "Mixed" as the type of blood for fish; that is a printing slip, since a fish heart carries only deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated at the gills.

rows.stem: In xylem tissue, vessels and tracheids of the roots, stems and leaves are interconnected to form a continuous system of water-conducting channels reaching all parts of the plant. Explain how this is achieved.
rows.solution:
Two forces move water up through the continuous system of xylem channels.

Root pressure: the cells of the root in contact with the soil actively take up ions. This creates a difference in the concentration of ions between the root and the soil, so water moves into the root from the soil to eliminate the difference. There is thus a steady movement of water into the root xylem, creating a column of water that is pushed upwards.

Transpirational pull: water is lost as vapour through the stomata of the leaves and other aerial parts (transpiration). This loss creates a suction which pulls water from the xylem cells of the roots up through the stems to the leaves. Transpiration pull is the main force moving water in tall plants, especially during the day.

rows.stem: Show the cross and observations made by Mendel when he crossed pure tall pea plant with a pure short pea plant to get \(\mathrm{F_1}\) progeny.
rows.solution:
Let T stand for the factor for tallness and t for shortness.

Parents: pure tall TT \(\times\) pure short tt.

Gametes: T (from the tall parent) and t (from the short parent).

\(\mathrm{F_1}\): Tt, all tall plants.

Observations (any two):

1. No medium-height or short plants were found in the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation.

2. All the progeny resembled one of the parents, the tall one.

3. All the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants were tall.

rows.stem:
(i) Which process in these plants is minimised to help the plants survive in dry conditions ?

(ii) Which part of the leaf is responsible for exchange of gases during photosynthesis ?
rows.context: Not all plants carry out photosynthesis by the same mechanism. In most plants, it depends directly on gaseous carbon dioxide that diffuses into the leaf. However, some plants can store carbon dioxide in the vacuole of the leaf cells as part of a complex carbon compound. This compound is transported to the chloroplast and releases carbon dioxide when required for photosynthesis. This special mechanism is believed to have evolved as an adaptation in such plants which do not open stomata during the daytime to conserve water for survival in dry conditions (desert conditions).
rows.solution:
(i) Transpiration, the loss of water as water vapour, is minimised. These plants keep their stomata closed during the day, so little water is lost by evaporation from the leaves.

(ii) The stomata, the tiny pores in the epidermis of the leaf, through which carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.

rows.stem:
(i) List the events that occur during the process of photosynthesis.

(ii) When are such desert plants likely to take in carbon dioxide from the environment, unlike other plants ?

(iii) Draw a labelled diagram of stomata with open stomatal pore.
rows.context: Not all plants carry out photosynthesis by the same mechanism. In most plants, it depends directly on gaseous carbon dioxide that diffuses into the leaf. However, some plants can store carbon dioxide in the vacuole of the leaf cells as part of a complex carbon compound. This compound is transported to the chloroplast and releases carbon dioxide when required for photosynthesis. This special mechanism is believed to have evolved as an adaptation in such plants which do not open stomata during the daytime to conserve water for survival in dry conditions (desert conditions).
rows.solution:
(i) The events of photosynthesis are:

1. Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll.

2. Conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen.

3. Reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates.

(ii) At night. Their stomata open at night, so they take in carbon dioxide then and store it for use during the day.

(iii) Diagram: draw two bean-shaped (kidney-shaped) guard cells facing each other, with their inner walls curved apart to leave an open lens-shaped gap between them, set among the surrounding epidermal cells. Show small chloroplasts as dots inside the guard cells. Label the guard cells, the stomatal pore and the chloroplast.

rows.stem:
Observe the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :

(i) Give the name of the structure and type of reproduction shown in the above diagram.

(ii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of the above mentioned method of reproduction.

(iii) Give reason : Asexual reproduction lacks genetic variation.

(iv) Why have higher organisms resorted to sexual reproduction in spite of its complexity ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (i) asks to name the structure and the type of reproduction from a printed drawing carrying four labels: 'Adventitious bud', 'Young Plant', 'Marginal notch' and 'Leaf'; the plant is named nowhere in the text, and (ii) builds on (i). Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) The structure is the leaf of *Bryophyllum*, with buds produced in the notches along its margin. The type of reproduction is vegetative propagation, a form of asexual reproduction.

(ii) Advantage (any one): the new plants are genetically identical to the parent, so the desirable traits of the parent are maintained; or such plants bear flowers and fruits earlier than plants grown from seeds; or plants that have lost the capacity to produce seeds can still be propagated.

Disadvantage: there is no genetic variation in the offspring.

(iii) Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. The offspring are produced by mitosis from the DNA of the single parent, so they have the same genetic make-up as the parent and there is no variation (apart from small errors in DNA copying).

(iv) Sexual reproduction combines the DNA of two individuals, so it creates genetic variation among the offspring. Variation increases the chances of survival of the species in a changing environment and drives evolution.

rows.stem:
Observe the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :

(i) Give the name and type of reproduction shown in the above diagram.

(ii) Comment on the processes taking place in stage P.

(iii) Name an organism which reproduces by the above mentioned method.

(iv) Name the method that can be used to raise plants that have lost their capacity to produce seeds. List any two advantages of growing plants by such a method.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (i)-(iii) depend on a printed three-stage sequence joined by arrows: a single cell labelled Nucleus, Cytoplasm, Cell and Cyst (Protective wall), then a stage labelled P, then a final stage; what happens at P is shown only in the drawing and is withheld here because it names the process asked in (i). Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) The process is multiple fission, a type of asexual reproduction.

(ii) In stage P, inside the protective cyst, the nucleus divides repeatedly and the nuclear divisions are followed by divisions of the cytoplasm. So many daughter cells are formed at the same time; when the cyst bursts, they are released.

(iii) *Plasmodium* (the malarial parasite).

(iv) Vegetative propagation.

Any two advantages: all the plants produced are genetically similar to the parent plant, so its desirable characters are kept; such plants bear flowers and fruits earlier than those produced from seeds; plants such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine, which have lost the capacity to produce seeds, can be propagated.

rows.stem: Which of the following is an example of a displacement reaction ?

options.label: A
options.text: The combustion of natural gas

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction of a reactive metal with dilute acid

options.label: C
options.text: The electrolysis of water

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction of quick lime with water

rows.solution:
A displacement reaction is one in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound. A reactive metal such as zinc displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid:

\(\mathrm{Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2}\)

Combustion of natural gas, electrolysis of water and the reaction of quick lime with water are combustion, decomposition and combination reactions respectively.

This is option (B) The reaction of a reactive metal with dilute acid.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
rows.stem: To a small amount of copper oxide in a beaker, when we add dilute hydrochloric acid slowly with stirring, the change in the colour of the solution is due to the formation of :

options.label: A
options.text: Copper(II) oxide, which is black in colour.

options.label: B
options.text: Copper(I) chloride, which is blue in colour.

options.label: C
options.text: Copper(II) chloride, which is blue-green in colour.

options.label: D
options.text: Copper(I) oxide, which is black in colour.

rows.solution:
Copper oxide is a base and reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give copper(II) chloride and water:

\(\mathrm{CuO + 2HCl \rightarrow CuCl_2 + H_2O}\)

The copper(II) chloride formed makes the solution blue-green.

This is option (C) Copper(II) chloride, which is blue-green in colour.

rows.stem:
In the following equation

\(\mathrm{x\,KI + H_2O_2 \longrightarrow I_2 + y\,KOH}\)

x and y respectively are :
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{I_2}\) has two iodine atoms, so 2 KI are needed. That gives 2 potassium atoms on the left, so 2 KOH are formed:

\(\mathrm{2KI + H_2O_2 \rightarrow I_2 + 2KOH}\)

Check: hydrogen 2 = 2 and oxygen 2 = 2. So x and y are 2 and 2, which is option (A) 2, 2.

rows.stem:
Consider the structures ‘X’ and ‘Y’ given below :

Which of the following statements are correct ?

(i) ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are homologues.

(ii) ‘X’ and ‘Y’ have the same structural formula, but different molecular formula.

(iii) ‘X’ and ‘Y’ have the same molecular formula, but different structural formula.

(iv) ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are structural isomers.

options.label: A
options.text: (i) and (iii)

options.label: B
options.text: (i) and (iv)

options.label: C
options.text: (ii) and (iv)

options.label: D
options.text: (iii) and (iv)

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - 'X' and 'Y' are printed only as full structural formulas with every hydrogen drawn; naming them or describing their carbon skeletons would state the answer, so they are not described. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
X is a straight chain of four carbon atoms with ten hydrogen atoms (butane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\)). Y has three carbon atoms in a chain with the fourth carbon branching from the middle one, also with ten hydrogen atoms (isobutane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\)).

They have the same molecular formula but different structures, so statements (iii) and (iv) are correct: they are structural isomers. They are not homologues, which differ by a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) unit, and their structural formulas are not the same.

This is option (D) (iii) and (iv).

rows.stem: The reaction of calcium with cold water is :

options.label: A
options.text: Less violent, but the heat evolved is sufficient for the hydrogen to catch fire.

options.label: B
options.text: Very violent and exothermic and hydrogen catches fire.

options.label: C
options.text: Exothermic, but the heat evolved is not sufficient for the hydrogen to catch fire.

options.label: D
options.text: Slow and endothermic.

rows.solution:
Calcium reacts with cold water less violently than sodium or potassium. The reaction is exothermic, but the heat evolved is not sufficient for the hydrogen to catch fire; the bubbles of hydrogen stick to the metal and calcium starts floating.

\(\mathrm{Ca + 2H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + H_2}\)

This is option (C) Exothermic, but the heat evolved is not sufficient for the hydrogen to catch fire.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
rows.stem: In which case/cases will the bulb glow considering that all other connections of electric circuit are complete and working ?

options.label: A
options.text: Case (i) only

options.label: B
options.text: Case (ii) only

options.label: C
options.text: Cases (ii) and (iii)

options.label: D
options.text: Case (iii) only

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the three set-ups (i), (ii) and (iii) are given only as a drawing: in each, a battery, a bulb and a switch are wired to two iron nails fixed through a rubber cork at the bottom of a beaker, and the beaker holds glucose solution in (i), alcohol solution in (ii) and dilute HCl in (iii). Which liquid is in which case is labelled only in the drawing. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
The bulb glows only if the liquid in the beaker conducts electricity, which needs ions. Dilute hydrochloric acid produces \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions in solution, so it conducts. Glucose and alcohol contain hydrogen but do not produce \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions in solution, so they do not conduct.

The bulb glows with dilute HCl alone, which is option (D) Case (iii) only.

rows.stem: When zinc reacts with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), the product formed is :

options.label: A
options.text: \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\mathrm{ZnO}\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\mathrm{Na_2ZnO_2}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\mathrm{Zn(OH)_2}\)

rows.solution:
Zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium zincate, and hydrogen gas is given off:

\(\mathrm{2NaOH + Zn \rightarrow Na_2ZnO_2 + H_2}\)

This is option (C) \(\mathrm{Na_2ZnO_2}\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** There are large number of compounds with many carbon atoms linked to each other.

**Reason (R) :** Carbon-Carbon bond is very strong and stable.
rows.context: For Question number 24, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to this question from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Carbon forms a large number of compounds with long chains of carbon atoms linked to each other (catenation), so the Assertion is true. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and hence stable, which is what allows carbon to form such large chains, so the Reason is true and explains the Assertion.

Both are true and the Reason is the correct explanation, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Show the formation of the following ionic compounds by transfer of electrons between the combining atoms :

(i) Sodium oxide \((\mathrm{Na_2O})\)

(ii) Magnesium chloride \((\mathrm{MgCl_2})\)

(Given : Atomic number : Na = 11, Mg = 12, O = 8, Cl = 17)
rows.solution:
(i) Sodium (2, 8, 1) has one electron in its outermost shell, and oxygen (2, 6) needs two more. Each of two sodium atoms transfers its one valence electron to the oxygen atom:

\(\mathrm{2Na \rightarrow 2Na^+ + 2e^-}\)

\(\mathrm{O + 2e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}}\)

In the electron dot diagram, each Na is drawn with one dot, and an arrow carries each dot to the O atom (shown with its 6 electrons). The product is two \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) ions and one oxide ion, \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), in brackets with a complete octet: \(\mathrm{(Na^+)_2(O^{2-})}\), that is \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\).

(ii) Magnesium (2, 8, 2) has two electrons in its outermost shell, and chlorine (2, 8, 7) needs one more. Magnesium transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms:

\(\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}\)

\(\mathrm{2Cl + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-}\)

In the electron dot diagram, Mg is drawn with two dots, and an arrow carries one dot to each of two Cl atoms (each shown with its 7 electrons). The product is \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions, each in brackets with a complete octet: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}(Cl^-)_2}\), that is \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\).

rows.stem: 2 g of green coloured crystals of ferrous sulphate are heated in a dry boiling tube. Name the type of chemical reaction taking place. Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction. Is this an exothermic or an endothermic reaction ?
rows.solution:
The reaction is a thermal decomposition reaction. On heating, the green crystals first lose their water of crystallisation; then the ferrous sulphate decomposes into ferric oxide, sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide, and a smell of burning sulphur is noticed.

\(\mathrm{2FeSO_4(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Fe_2O_3(s) + SO_2(g) + SO_3(g)}\)

Check: iron 2 = 2, sulphur 2 = 1 + 1, oxygen 8 = 3 + 2 + 3. An unbalanced equation loses half a mark.

It is an endothermic reaction, since heat has to be supplied continuously for the decomposition to take place.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
rows.stem:
Give reasons :

(i) For dilution of an acid, acid is added into water and not water into acid.

(ii) Dry \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas does not turn blue litmus red whereas dilute hydrochloric acid does.

(iii) Blue colour of Copper(II) sulphate crystals turns white on heating.
rows.solution:
(i) Diluting an acid is highly exothermic. When acid is added slowly to water, the large amount of water absorbs the heat, so there is no excessive local heating. If water is added to concentrated acid, the heat generated can make the mixture splash out and cause burns, and the glass container may break.

(ii) Acidic behaviour is due to \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions. Dry HCl gas does not ionise and produces no \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions, so it does not turn blue litmus red. In dilute hydrochloric acid, HCl ionises in water and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions are present, so it turns blue litmus red.

(iii) Blue copper(II) sulphate crystals contain five molecules of water of crystallisation. On heating they lose this water and become white anhydrous copper sulphate:

\(\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} CuSO_4 + 5H_2O}\)

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem:
Write the preparation of the following compounds with balanced chemical equation :

(i) \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) by chlor-alkali process

(ii) Baking Soda

(iii) Plaster of Paris
rows.solution:
(i) Sodium hydroxide: electricity is passed through brine, an aqueous solution of sodium chloride. It decomposes to form sodium hydroxide; chlorine gas is given off at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode.

\(\mathrm{2NaCl(aq) + 2H_2O(l) \xrightarrow{\text{electricity}} 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g) + Cl_2(g)}\)

(ii) Baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate): carbon dioxide and ammonia are passed through a cold solution of sodium chloride. Sodium hydrogen carbonate separates out and ammonium chloride remains in solution.

\(\mathrm{NaCl + H_2O + NH_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow NaHCO_3 + NH_4Cl}\)

(iii) Plaster of Paris: gypsum is heated at 373 K. It loses part of its water of crystallisation and becomes calcium sulphate hemihydrate.

\(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O \xrightarrow{373\,K} CaSO_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}H_2O + 1\frac{1}{2}H_2O}\)

The marking scheme deducts half a mark for each equation that is not balanced.

rows.stem: Define anode mud.
rows.context: An electrochemical process is used for refining metals by selectively dissolving and depositing them through electrolysis. Electrolytic refining is used for metals like Copper, Zinc, Tin, Nickel, Silver and Gold.
rows.solution: During electrolytic refining of a metal, the insoluble impurities settle down at the bottom of the anode. This deposit is called anode mud.

rows.stem: In electrolytic refining of copper, name the anode and the cathode.
rows.context: An electrochemical process is used for refining metals by selectively dissolving and depositing them through electrolysis. Electrolytic refining is used for metals like Copper, Zinc, Tin, Nickel, Silver and Gold.
rows.solution: The anode is a rod (thick block) of impure copper and the cathode is a thin strip of pure copper. The electrolyte is acidified copper sulphate solution.

rows.stem: With the help of chemical equations, show the extraction of copper from its ore \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\).
rows.context: An electrochemical process is used for refining metals by selectively dissolving and depositing them through electrolysis. Electrolytic refining is used for metals like Copper, Zinc, Tin, Nickel, Silver and Gold.
rows.solution:
Copper glance, \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\), is heated in air. Part of it is converted to copper(I) oxide:

\(\mathrm{2Cu_2S + 3O_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2Cu_2O(s) + 2SO_2(g)}\)

The copper(I) oxide then reacts with the remaining copper(I) sulphide to give copper metal:

\(\mathrm{2Cu_2O + Cu_2S \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 6Cu(s) + SO_2(g)}\)

rows.stem: Draw a neat and labelled diagram showing electrolytic refining of copper.
rows.context: An electrochemical process is used for refining metals by selectively dissolving and depositing them through electrolysis. Electrolytic refining is used for metals like Copper, Zinc, Tin, Nickel, Silver and Gold.
rows.solution:
Diagram: draw a tank containing acidified copper sulphate solution. Dip a thick rod of impure copper into it as the anode, connected to the positive terminal of a battery, and a thin strip of pure copper as the cathode, connected to the negative terminal through a key. Show \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions moving through the solution towards the cathode, and the insoluble impurities collected at the bottom below the anode.

Label: cathode (pure copper), anode (impure copper), acidified copper sulphate solution, tank, impurities (anode mud), battery and key.

rows.stem:
(i) What is homologous series ? Which two of the following organic compounds belong to the same homologous series ?

\(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\), \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\), \(\mathrm{C_3H_4}\), \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\)

(ii) Write the product(s) in the following reactions :

(I) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH + CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{\text{Acid}}}\)

(II) \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Burning}}}\)

(iii) Why does micelle formation take place when soap is added to water ?
rows.solution:
(i) A homologous series is a series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain. Its members can be represented by one general formula, and successive members differ by a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) unit (14 u).

\(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) and \(\mathrm{C_4H_8}\) belong to the same homologous series: both are alkenes, of general formula \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}\). (\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) is an alkane and \(\mathrm{C_3H_4}\) an alkyne.)

(ii) (I) Ethanol and ethanoic acid react in the presence of an acid to give an ester, ethyl ethanoate, and water (esterification):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH + CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{\text{Acid}} CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

(II) Ethanol burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Burning}} 2CO_2 + 3H_2O}\)

(iii) A soap molecule has an ionic end that is attracted to water and a long hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in oil or grease but not in water. In water the tails turn away from the water and cluster together at the centre, with the ionic ends facing outwards towards the water. This cluster of molecules is the micelle, and the oily dirt collects in its centre.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the following compounds :

(I) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

(II) \(\mathrm{CH_3-C\equiv C-H}\)

(ii) Name the reaction which is commonly used in the conversion of vegetable oils to fats.

(iii) Why is the melting point of \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) higher than \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\) ?

(iv) What happens when a piece of sodium is dropped into ethanol ?

(v) Write the products in the following reaction :

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5 + NaOH \longrightarrow}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - (i) prints the two compounds as structural formulas: (I) a carbon double-bonded to O and joined to two \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups, (II) a \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) group drawn with all three hydrogens, joined to a carbon triple-bonded to a carbon carrying one H. The stem carries the same compounds as condensed formulas, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) (I) Propanone (acetone). (II) Propyne.

(ii) Hydrogenation, an addition reaction: hydrogen is added to the vegetable oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst.

(iii) \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) has a higher molecular mass than \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\), and in a homologous series the melting point increases with molecular mass. So \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\) has the higher melting point.

(iv) Sodium reacts with ethanol to form sodium ethoxide, and hydrogen gas is evolved:

\(\mathrm{2Na + 2CH_3CH_2OH \rightarrow 2CH_3CH_2O^-Na^+ + H_2}\)

(v) The ester is converted back to the alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid (saponification):

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5 + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3COONa + C_2H_5OH}\)

The products are sodium ethanoate and ethanol.

rows.stem: The correct way to connect an ammeter and a voltmeter in an electric circuit is :

options.label: A
options.text: Ammeter in parallel and voltmeter in series

options.label: B
options.text: Ammeter and voltmeter both in parallel

options.label: C
options.text: Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel

options.label: D
options.text: Ammeter and voltmeter both in series

rows.solution:
An ammeter measures the current through a circuit, so it is connected in series. A voltmeter measures the potential difference across two points, so it is connected in parallel across them.

This is option (C) Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem:
Observe the given ray diagram showing refraction through a prism and choose the correct option for colour of rays 1 and 2 :

*Colour of ray 1*, *Colour of ray 2*

options.label: A
options.text: Blue, Red

options.label: B
options.text: Green, Yellow

options.label: C
options.text: Red, Violet

options.label: D
options.text: Violet, Red

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a ray labelled 'White light' enters face AB of a triangular glass prism ABC and two emergent rays labelled 1 and 2 leave face AC; which of the two is deviated more is shown only in the drawing and is withheld here because it is the answer. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
In a prism, red light bends the least and violet the most. Ray 1 is deviated less than ray 2, so ray 1 is red and ray 2 is violet.

This is option (C) Red, Violet.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The needle of a compass, kept in an external magnetic field, always aligns itself in the North-South direction of the Earth.

**Reason (R) :** The behaviour of the needle of the compass is similar to the behaviour of a freely suspended bar magnet.
rows.context: For Question number 32, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to this question from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
A compass needle kept in an external magnetic field aligns itself along the direction of that field, which need not be the North-South direction of the earth. The Assertion is false.

The compass needle is a small bar magnet, so it behaves like a freely suspended bar magnet. The Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.stem:
A ray of light enters into medium B from medium A as shown in the given figure :

(a) Which one of these two media is optically denser than the other medium ? Justify your answer.

(b) If the speed of light in medium A is \(\mathrm{V_A}\) and in medium B is \(\mathrm{V_B}\), then what is the refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a vertical line separates medium A (lower left) from medium B (upper right), with the normal NN' drawn dashed and horizontal; a ray from medium A meets the boundary where the normal crosses it and continues into medium B. Whether it bends towards or away from the normal is shown only in the drawing and is withheld here because it decides (a). Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(a) Medium A is optically denser. On entering medium B the ray bends away from the normal NN', and light bends away from the normal when it passes from a denser medium into a rarer one.

(b) The refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A is

\(n_{BA} = \dfrac{\text{speed of light in medium A}}{\text{speed of light in medium B}} = \dfrac{V_A}{V_B}\).

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: What happens when light is scattered from (i) very fine particles and (ii) very large size particles of medium ? Justify your answer in each case.
rows.solution:
(i) Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light. The particles are so small that they scatter light of shorter wavelengths much more than light of longer wavelengths, and blue has a short wavelength.

(ii) With very large particles the scattered light may appear white. Large particles scatter light of all wavelengths about equally.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem: With the help of a ray diagram, explain any phenomenon of formation of spectrum in nature.
rows.solution:
A rainbow is a natural spectrum formed when sunlight passes through tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. Each droplet acts like a small prism: it refracts and disperses the incident sunlight, then reflects it internally, and finally refracts it again as it comes out of the drop, so the different colours emerge separated.

Diagram: draw a circular raindrop and a ray of white sunlight entering it. Show the light splitting into its colours on entering, reflecting from the back surface of the drop, and leaving the drop spread out, with red and violet rays marked separately. Label the white sunlight, the raindrop, and the red and violet rays, and draw arrows on the rays.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
rows.stem:
Study the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :

(a) Write the name of the eye defect shown in the diagram. Where is the image formed in this eye defect with respect to the retina of the eye ?

(b) List two causes of this eye defect.

(c) With the help of a diagram, show how this eye defect of vision is corrected.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the defect exists only in the drawing: an eye (lens and eyeball) with two points N and N' marked on the axis in front of it and rays from N' entering the eye and meeting at a point; which of N and N' is nearer the eye, and where the rays meet relative to the retina, are withheld here since they decide the defect. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(a) The defect is hypermetropia (far-sightedness). The near point of the eye has moved farther away, to N, so light from an object at the normal near point N' is focused behind the retina.

(b) Two causes:

1. The focal length of the eye lens is too long.

2. The eyeball has become too small.

(c) It is corrected with a convex lens of suitable power. Diagram: place a convex lens in front of the eye. Rays from an object at N' are converged by the lens so that they appear to come from N, the near point of the defective eye. The eye lens then brings them to a focus on the retina. Show the rays from N' bending at the convex lens, the dotted lines produced back to N, and the rays meeting on the retina.

rows.stem:
(a) Name a device which is used to :

(i) Maintain a constant potential difference in a circuit.

(ii) Change the electric current in an electric circuit.

(b) When the potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 110 V, a current of 5 A flows through it. What will be the value of current flowing through it when the potential difference is increased to 220 V ?
rows.solution:
(a) (i) A battery (or an electric cell) maintains a constant potential difference.

(ii) A rheostat (a variable resistance) changes the current in a circuit.

(b) Resistance of the heater: \(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{110}{5} = 22\,\Omega\).

At 220 V the current is \(I' = \dfrac{V'}{R} = \dfrac{220}{22} = 10\) A.

(Equally, by Ohm's law the current is directly proportional to the potential difference, so doubling the potential difference doubles the current from 5 A to 10 A.)

rows.stem:
Consider the given electric circuit :

Calculate the following :

(a) Total resistance of the circuit

(b) The electric current drawn from the battery

(c) Potential difference between points P and Q
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the circuit is given only as a drawing: points P, Q, R and S, resistors of \(1\,\Omega\), \(2\,\Omega\), \(3\,\Omega\) and \(4\,\Omega\) and two of \(5\,\Omega\), a 10 V battery, a key and an ammeter; which resistors lie between R and S, which between P and Q, and how each group is connected decide every answer and are withheld here. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
(a) Between R and S: the \(4\,\Omega\) and \(1\,\Omega\) resistors are in series, \(4 + 1 = 5\,\Omega\), and this is in parallel with the \(5\,\Omega\) resistor joining R and S directly:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_1} = \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5}\), so \(R_1 = \dfrac{5}{2}\,\Omega\).

Between P and Q: the \(2\,\Omega\) and \(3\,\Omega\) resistors are in series, \(2 + 3 = 5\,\Omega\), and this is in parallel with the \(5\,\Omega\) resistor joining P and Q directly:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_2} = \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5}\), so \(R_2 = \dfrac{5}{2}\,\Omega\).

The two groups are in series with the battery, so the total resistance is \(R = R_1 + R_2 = \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{5}{2} = 5\,\Omega\).

(b) Current drawn from the battery: \(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\) A.

(c) The whole current of 2 A passes through the combination between P and Q, so the potential difference between P and Q is \(V = IR_2 = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 5\) V.

rows.subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
rows.stem: Without calculation, find out the focal length of the given convex lens. Justify your answer.
rows.context:
The variation of image distance \((v)\) with the object distance \((u)\) for a convex lens is given in the following observation table. Analyse it and answer the questions given below :

| S.No. | Object distance \((u)\) cm | Image distance \((v)\) cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(-150\) | \(+30\) |
| 2 | \(-75\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
| 3 | \(-50\) | \(+50\) |
| 4 | \(-37{\cdot}5\) | \(+75\) |
| 5 | \(-30\) | \(+150\) |
| 6 | \(-15\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
rows.solution: The focal length is 25 cm (\(f = +25\) cm). In observation 3 the object distance equals the image distance, 50 cm. For a convex lens this happens only when the object is at 2F, so \(2f = 50\) cm and \(f = 25\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
rows.stem: Which one of the observations given in the table is not correct and why ?
rows.context:
The variation of image distance \((v)\) with the object distance \((u)\) for a convex lens is given in the following observation table. Analyse it and answer the questions given below :

| S.No. | Object distance \((u)\) cm | Image distance \((v)\) cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(-150\) | \(+30\) |
| 2 | \(-75\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
| 3 | \(-50\) | \(+50\) |
| 4 | \(-37{\cdot}5\) | \(+75\) |
| 5 | \(-30\) | \(+150\) |
| 6 | \(-15\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
rows.solution:
Observation 6 is not correct. With \(u = -15\) cm the object is between the optical centre and the focus (\(f = 25\) cm). The image is then formed on the same side of the lens as the object (virtual and erect), so the image distance must be negative, not \(+37{\cdot}5\) cm.

Check by the lens formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{2}{75}\), so \(v = -37{\cdot}5\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
rows.stem: Find out the value of magnification for \(u = -30\) cm. Write the nature of the image formed. Give reason for your answer.
rows.context:
The variation of image distance \((v)\) with the object distance \((u)\) for a convex lens is given in the following observation table. Analyse it and answer the questions given below :

| S.No. | Object distance \((u)\) cm | Image distance \((v)\) cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(-150\) | \(+30\) |
| 2 | \(-75\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
| 3 | \(-50\) | \(+50\) |
| 4 | \(-37{\cdot}5\) | \(+75\) |
| 5 | \(-30\) | \(+150\) |
| 6 | \(-15\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
rows.solution:
For \(u = -30\) cm the table gives \(v = +150\) cm.

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{150}{-30} = -5\).

The image is real and inverted (and five times enlarged), because the value of m is negative.

rows.stem: Analyse the data given in the table above and draw the labelled ray diagram for \(u = -30\) cm and \(v = 150\) cm.
rows.context:
The variation of image distance \((v)\) with the object distance \((u)\) for a convex lens is given in the following observation table. Analyse it and answer the questions given below :

| S.No. | Object distance \((u)\) cm | Image distance \((v)\) cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(-150\) | \(+30\) |
| 2 | \(-75\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
| 3 | \(-50\) | \(+50\) |
| 4 | \(-37{\cdot}5\) | \(+75\) |
| 5 | \(-30\) | \(+150\) |
| 6 | \(-15\) | \(+37{\cdot}5\) |
rows.solution:
With \(f = 25\) cm, the object at 30 cm lies between F and 2F, and the image at 150 cm lies beyond 2F on the other side of the lens.

Ray diagram: draw a convex lens with its principal axis and mark \(\mathrm{F_1}\), \(\mathrm{2F_1}\) on the object side and \(\mathrm{F_2}\), \(\mathrm{2F_2}\) on the other. Place the object AB between \(\mathrm{F_1}\) and \(\mathrm{2F_1}\). From A draw a ray parallel to the principal axis; after refraction it passes through \(\mathrm{F_2}\). Draw a second ray from A through the optical centre O, which goes on undeviated. The two refracted rays meet below the axis beyond \(\mathrm{2F_2}\) at A'. Draw the image A'B' there: real, inverted and enlarged. Label A, B, A', B', O, F and 2F on both sides, and draw arrows on the rays: the marking scheme deducts half a mark if they are missing or wrong.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem:
(i) What is a solenoid ? Draw a diagram showing the magnetic field pattern due to a current-carrying solenoid (inside and outside).

(ii) Name any two factors on which the magnitude of the magnetic field due to a current-carrying solenoid depends.

(iii) A current-carrying solenoid is stretched and converted into a straight wire carrying current. Draw a diagram showing the magnetic field pattern around it and mark the direction of the magnetic field.
rows.solution:
(i) A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder.

Diagram: draw the solenoid connected to a battery and a key. Inside the solenoid draw straight, parallel, equally spaced field lines along its axis (the field inside is uniform). Outside, draw closed curves leaving one end and returning to the other, as around a bar magnet. Mark arrows: outside the solenoid the lines run from its north end to its south end, and inside from the south end to the north end.

(ii) Any two: the current flowing through the solenoid; the number of turns of the coil; the nature of the core material.

(iii) Around the straight current-carrying wire the field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it. Diagram: draw a straight vertical wire with an arrow showing the current upwards, and concentric circles around it with arrows anticlockwise when seen from above. The direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule: if the thumb points along the current, the curled fingers give the direction of the field. A current drawn the other way, with the field marked in the matching direction, is equally correct.

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of a diagram, show that a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field, experiences a force. Indicate the direction of the field, current and force clearly.

(ii) The diagram given below shows an electron moving in a uniform magnetic field.

(I) What will be the direction of the force acting on the electron ?

(II) What will happen to the direction of the force acting on the electron, if the direction of the magnetic field as well as the direction of motion of the electron, both are reversed ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - (ii) the drawing shows four parallel horizontal field lines with arrowheads, labelled 'Magnetic field', crossed by a vertical line with an arrowhead labelled 'Electron'; the direction of the field and of the electron's motion are given only by these arrowheads and are withheld here, since together they decide (ii)(I). Page idx 30.
rows.solution:
(i) Set-up: suspend a small aluminium rod AB horizontally from a stand by two connecting wires, so that it lies between the two poles of a horseshoe magnet, with the north pole below the rod and the south pole above it. The field between the poles is then vertically upwards. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat.

Pass a current through the rod from B to A: the rod is displaced sideways. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the displacement. So the current-carrying conductor experiences a force in the magnetic field.

Diagram: draw the magnet, the rod and the circuit, and mark three arrows: the magnetic field upwards from the N pole to the S pole, the current along the rod from B to A, and the force on the rod, perpendicular to both the rod and the field. The direction of the force follows Fleming's left-hand rule: with the forefinger along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the force.

(ii) (I) The field points to the left and the electron moves upwards, so the conventional current is downwards, opposite to the electron's motion. By Fleming's left-hand rule, with the forefinger to the left and the middle finger downwards, the thumb points into the plane of the paper. The force on the electron is into the plane of the paper.

(II) Reversing the field reverses the force, and reversing the motion of the electron reverses it again. With both reversed, the direction of the force remains the same.
